topic.subject: science
topic.title: Is matter around us pure
topic.scope: mixtures vs compounds, solutions, suspensions, colloids, concentration, separation techniques, elements

misconceptions.statement: Anything that is not contaminated or dirty is a pure substance.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the scientific definition of 'pure' with the common usage of the word in daily life (e.g., pure milk, pure gold).
misconceptions.fix: In science, a pure substance consists of only one type of particle, whereas a mixture contains two or more substances mixed in any proportion.

probe.question: Is a glass of 'pure' milk from a dairy a pure substance?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is natural and has no added impurities.

misconceptions.statement: If a mixture looks clear and uniform, it must be a solution.
misconceptions.why: Students rely on visual observation rather than the particle size or the Tyndall effect to classify mixtures.
misconceptions.fix: Some mixtures, like colloids, appear uniform to the naked eye but contain particles large enough to scatter light.

probe.question: Does a clear-looking colloid like milk show the Tyndall effect?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it looks uniform and clear like a solution.

misconceptions.statement: Evaporation can separate all components of a mixture.
misconceptions.why: Students overgeneralize the success of separating salt from water to all types of mixtures.
misconceptions.fix: Evaporation only works for separating a volatile solvent from a non-volatile solute; it cannot separate two liquids or solids effectively.

probe.question: Can you separate a mixture of acetone and water using evaporation?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, just heat it and the water will evaporate leaving the acetone behind.

misconceptions.statement: A compound is just a mixture of elements that are stuck together.
misconceptions.why: Students fail to distinguish between physical mixing and chemical bonding, assuming the properties of the elements remain unchanged.
misconceptions.fix: In a compound, elements are chemically combined in a fixed ratio, resulting in a new substance with entirely different properties than its constituent elements.

probe.question: Does iron in iron sulphide still show magnetic properties?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because iron is still present in the compound.
